Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Protesters draped themselves in the colorful flag of Tibet and shouted slogans at the Chinese embassy in London on Saturday at the start of a demonstration to mark the 50th anniversary since the Tibetan uprising against China. Protesters have gathered in London to mark the 50th anniversary of the Tibet uprising. "Tibetans in Tibet -- we are with you!" they shouted. "China, China, China -- out, out, out!" The small but fervent group marched from the embassy through west London to Trafalgar Square, where they were due to hear a speech by Thomas Shao Jiang, a Chinese dissident who was one of the student organizers of the Tiananmen Square protest in Beijing in 1989. "I think it's important that Tibet is kept in the world's eye," protester Chris Last told CNN amid placards declaring "50 years too long" and "We are Tibetans, not Chinese." While Tibet is technically autonomous from the central Chinese government, its current government is directed from Beijing. The Dalai Lama, traditionally the spiritual and political leader of the Tibetan Buddhists, lives in exile in India. Tuesday marks the 50th anniversary of a failed 1959 uprising against Beijing's rule that sent the Dalai Lama into exile. Protest organizers said the march was meant to draw public attention to what they say is a deepening crisis a year after China cracked down on protests across Tibet. "(British Prime Minister) Gordon Brown and other world leaders must respond urgently and publicly to the Tibet crisis by taking immediate action," said Stephanie Brigden, director of Free Tibet. "They should demand that China calls off its security stranglehold in Tibet as an essential first step towards backing the Dalai Lama's initiative in finding a long-term and negotiated settlement to China's occupation." Tibetan Buddhists say they resent the slow erosion of their culture amid an influx of Han Chinese, the largest ethnic group in China. That resentment spilled over last March, when Buddhist monks initiated peaceful anti-Chinese protests in the regional capital, Lhasa, on the 49th anniversary of the uprising. The protests soon turned violent, with demonstrators burning vehicles and shops. Some protesters advocated independence from China, while others demonstrated against the growing influence of the Han Chinese in the area and other regions of China with ethnic Tibetan populations. The subsequent crackdown left 18 civilians and one police officer dead, according to the Chinese government. Tibet's self-proclaimed government-in-exile put the death toll from the protests at 140. China accuses the Dalai Lama of fomenting the discord in his homeland -- a charge he denies. "The Dalai Lama demanded the establishment of the so-called 'Greater Tibetan area' on a quarter of the Chinese territory, to drive away Chinese army stationed there guarding the Chinese territory, and to drive away Chinese people of other ethnic groups who lived there for generations. Is such a person a religious figure?" Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi said Saturday. "The conflict between him and us is not religious conflict, human rights conflict, ethnic conflict, nor cultural conflict," Yang said. "The conflict is whether or not to maintain China's unification, and whether or not to permit Tibet to be separated from the Chinese territory." The Dalai Lama has said he does not advocate violence or a separate and independent Tibet. He has said he wants a genuine autonomy that preserves the cultural heritage of the region. "I'm just disgusted with the way the Chinese behave towards the Tibetans. Even if you accept that Tibet has been swallowed up by China, why can't they give to them autonomy, respect their religion, their culture?" protester Bob Hunt said Saturday. "These are peaceable people, one of the most peaceable people in the world." Protester Shobha Trivedi said she hoped the protest march would make people more aware of the situation inside Tibet. "I feel as a human being, what (the) Chinese are doing for 50 years, nobody's bothering with it," she said. "And it's a real shame on everyone."

# Tibetans and Supporters Rally in London to Mark 50th Anniversary of Uprising Against China

**LONDON** — Hundreds of Tibetans, human rights activists, and supporters gathered in central London on Tuesday to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the failed 1959 uprising against Chinese rule in Tibet, waving Tibetan flags and calling for greater international attention to the region's political situation.

The demonstration, which began outside the Chinese Embassy before moving toward Downing Street, drew a diverse crowd chanting slogans and carrying banners reading "Free Tibet" and "China Out of Tibet." Many protesters wore traditional Tibetan clothing, while others held photographs of the Dalai Lama, the spiritual leader who fled into exile following the 1959 revolt.

## Voices from the Crowd

For many participants, the anniversary carried deep personal significance.

"My grandparents fled Tibet in 1959, and they never saw their homeland again," said Tenzin Dolma, 27, who was born in India before moving to Britain. "We are here today not just to remember the past, but to demand a future where Tibetans can live freely in their own land."

Others emphasized the ongoing nature of their concerns.

"Fifty years have passed, and yet the fundamental issues remain unresolved," said Jamyang Norbu, a community organizer who helped coordinate the event. "We continue to see restrictions on religious freedom, on language, and on the basic rights of the Tibetan people. The world cannot look away."

Non-Tibetan supporters also joined the demonstration. "This is about universal human rights," said British activist Sarah Whitmore, holding a candle in memory of those who died in the uprising. "When any group is denied its freedom, it concerns all of us."

## Historical Background

The 1959 uprising erupted in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa, amid growing tensions following China's assertion of control over the region in 1950. The revolt was suppressed, and the Dalai Lama subsequently fled to India, where he established a government-in-exile in Dharamsala. Tens of thousands of Tibetans followed him into exile in the years that followed.

Beijing maintains that its rule has brought development and modernization to Tibet, and describes the region as an integral part of China. Chinese officials have repeatedly characterized the Dalai Lama as a separatist seeking to divide the country—a charge the exiled leader has denied, stating he seeks meaningful autonomy rather than full independence.

## Official Responses

A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London responded to the protest with a statement reaffirming Beijing's position.

"Tibet has been an inseparable part of China since ancient times," the statement read. "Over the past decades, Tibet has achieved remarkable progress in economic and social development, and the rights of people of all ethnic groups are fully protected under the law. We firmly oppose any attempt to interfere in China's internal affairs under the pretext of human rights."

British lawmakers offered a range of responses. One Member of Parliament who addressed the crowd called for renewed diplomatic engagement.

"We must encourage genuine dialogue between the Chinese government and representatives of the Tibetan people," the MP said. "Britain has a long-standing commitment to human rights, and we cannot remain silent on these issues."

A spokesperson for the Foreign Office said the British government "continues to raise concerns about the human rights situation in Tibet through appropriate channels" while maintaining that Britain "regards Tibet as part of the People's Republic of China."

## A Continuing Cause

As the demonstration wound down in the late afternoon, organizers vowed to continue their advocacy.

"Every year we gather, and every year our numbers include a new generation," Dolma said. "We will not forget, and we will not stop until our voices are heard."

The London event was one of several similar demonstrations held in cities around the world to mark the anniversary, including in New York, Paris, and Dharamsala.

---

# Tibetan Communities Mark Anniversary of 1959 Uprising Amid Continued Tensions

## Demonstrations Held Worldwide

Each year on March 10, Tibetan exile communities and supporters around the world gather to commemorate the anniversary of the 1959 Tibetan uprising. Demonstrations typically occur in cities with significant Tibetan diaspora populations, including Dharamshala, India—home to the Tibetan government-in-exile—as well as New York, London, and other locations. Participants often carry Tibetan flags, display banners, and call for greater autonomy or independence and improved human rights conditions.

## Historical Background: The 1959 Uprising

The uprising began on March 10, 1959, in Lhasa, the Tibetan capital. Tensions had been building since 1950, when Chinese Communist forces entered Tibet, and following the 1951 Seventeen Point Agreement that formalized Chinese administration over the region.

The immediate trigger came amid fears that Chinese authorities planned to detain the 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, the spiritual and temporal leader of Tibetan Buddhism. Thousands of Tibetans surrounded the Dalai Lama's Norbulingka palace to protect him. The demonstrations escalated into broader unrest that was ultimately suppressed by Chinese forces, with significant casualties—though exact figures remain disputed between sources.

## The Dalai Lama's Exile

In the aftermath, the Dalai Lama fled Lhasa on the night of March 17, 1959, undertaking a difficult journey across the Himalayas into India. He was granted asylum by the Indian government and established a base in Dharamshala, where the Central Tibetan Administration (the government-in-exile) operates today.

Now in his late 80s, the Dalai Lama has for decades advocated what he calls the "Middle Way Approach," seeking genuine autonomy for Tibet within China rather than full independence. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989.

## China's Official Position

The Chinese government maintains that Tibet has been an integral part of China for centuries and characterizes its 1950s actions as a "peaceful liberation" that ended a feudal system. Beijing officially observes March 28 as "Serfs Emancipation Day," commemorating the reforms it says freed Tibetans from serfdom.

Chinese authorities describe the Dalai Lama as a separatist and reject the legitimacy of the government-in-exile. Officials point to infrastructure development, economic growth, and rising living standards as evidence of progress in the Tibet Autonomous Region.

## Ongoing Disputes

Human rights organizations and the exile community continue to raise concerns about religious restrictions, surveillance, cultural preservation, and the succession question surrounding the Dalai Lama—an issue where Beijing has asserted it will play a role in identifying his reincarnation, which the Dalai Lama and his followers reject.

The competing narratives surrounding these events remain a subject of significant international attention and debate.

---

*Note: This report presents multiple perspectives on a contested historical and political topic. Figures and characterizations vary considerably depending on sources.*

# Pro-Tibet Activists Rally Outside Chinese Embassy in London

**LONDON** — Dozens of pro-Tibet demonstrators gathered outside the Chinese Embassy in central London on Saturday, waving Tibetan flags and calling for greater autonomy and human rights protections for the Himalayan region.

The demonstration, organized by a coalition of Tibetan advocacy groups, drew activists of various ages who chanted slogans and held banners reading "Free Tibet" and "Human Rights Now." The gathering coincided with an anniversary significant to the Tibetan diaspora, though smaller demonstrations at the embassy occur periodically throughout the year.

## Voices from the Protest

Tenzin Dolkar, a demonstrator who said her family fled Tibet decades ago, described the protest as an act of preserving cultural identity.

"We are here to remind the world that Tibetans continue to face restrictions on their religious practices and language," she said. "This is about protecting our heritage and ensuring future generations know their history."

Organizers raised concerns about what they described as limitations on freedom of expression, religious worship, and the preservation of the Tibetan language in schools. Several speakers called on the British government to raise these issues in diplomatic discussions with Beijing.

"We're not asking for much—just the freedom for Tibetans to practice their faith and speak their language without fear," said one organizer addressing the crowd through a megaphone.

Free Tibet, a London-based advocacy organization, has long campaigned on these issues, calling for greater international attention to conditions inside the region.

## Beijing's Position

The Chinese government has consistently rejected such characterizations. In official statements, Beijing maintains that Tibet is an integral part of China and that its policies have brought significant economic development and improved living standards to the region.

Chinese officials have previously stated that religious freedom is protected under the country's constitution and that the government has invested heavily in infrastructure, healthcare, and education in the Tibet Autonomous Region. A spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry has, in past comments on similar demonstrations, described Tibet-related issues as "internal affairs" and cautioned against foreign interference.

"Tibet has enjoyed rapid economic growth and social stability," Chinese officials have said in previous statements, pointing to rising incomes and the preservation of cultural sites as evidence of successful governance.

Beijing frequently characterizes overseas pro-Tibet activism as being disconnected from the realities on the ground and has accused some advocacy groups of pursuing separatist agendas—a claim these organizations reject, saying they seek genuine autonomy rather than independence.

## A Long-Running Dispute

The status of Tibet remains one of the more contentious issues in China's relations with Western nations and human rights organizations. The Dalai Lama, the Tibetan spiritual leader who has lived in exile in India since 1959, advocates for what he calls a "Middle Way" approach seeking meaningful autonomy within China rather than full independence—a position Beijing views with suspicion.

The Metropolitan Police maintained a presence near the embassy during Saturday's demonstration, which remained peaceful. The protest dispersed by mid-afternoon without incident.

For participants, the gathering represented one of many ongoing efforts to keep international attention focused on their cause.

"Every time we stand here, we send a message that we haven't forgotten," Dolkar said. "And we won't stop."

The Chinese Embassy in London did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Saturday's demonstration.

---

**LONDON** — Thousands of pro-Tibet demonstrators marched through west London to Trafalgar Square on Saturday, waving the outlawed Tibetan flag and calling for greater autonomy and human rights protections in the Himalayan region.

The march, organized by the Free Tibet campaign group, wound its way through the streets of the capital, drawing supporters from across the United Kingdom and beyond. Demonstrators carried banners reading "Free Tibet" and "Stop the Killing in Tibet," while chanting slogans demanding international attention to the situation.

## Organizers Call for Sustained Pressure

Organizers estimated the crowd numbered in the thousands, describing the turnout as a powerful demonstration of solidarity.

"We are here today to show the world that Tibet has not been forgotten," said a spokesperson for Free Tibet. "The international community cannot continue to turn a blind eye. We are calling on governments everywhere to press for meaningful dialogue and to hold those responsible for human rights abuses accountable."

The organizers emphasized that the demonstration was peaceful and intended to raise awareness rather than provoke confrontation.

"This is about giving a voice to the voiceless," the spokesperson added. "The Tibetan people deserve the right to preserve their culture, their religion, and their way of life."

"I've been coming to these marches for years," said one protester, draped in a Tibetan flag. "It's important that we keep the pressure on. Every year we come out, and every year we hope things will change."

Another demonstrator, who traveled from northern England to attend, said the cause was deeply personal. "My friends have family in Tibet, and they can't speak freely about what's happening there. So we speak for them here, where we can."

Families with children, students, and members of Britain's Tibetan diaspora joined monks in traditional robes as the procession moved toward Trafalgar Square, where a rally featuring speeches and cultural performances was held.

## Beijing Responds

- Demonstrations that reportedly turned violent, with rioting, arson, and clashes
- Chinese state media emphasizing attacks on Han Chinese residents and property destruction

- Increased military and police presence in Tibetan areas

## Analysis and Outlook

The events of 2008 and their aftermath crystallized several enduring dynamics:
